say.text: A supine plain abdominal film. Loops sit centrally, and their folds cross the full width of the lumen in a stack-of-coins pattern.
Which bowel is this, and which marker tells you?
Tempting: valvulae conniventes are the first fold you learned, and the big bowel is the loop people expect to dilate.
But a fold does not name a bowel by itself. Check where these folds sit and whether they cross the lumen, then choose again.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the marker before the bowel: the fold that crosses the full width belongs to one bowel only.

say.text: Tempting: haustra are the folds you see most on a colon film, and these loops have folds, so the label feels right.
Look at the fold again. Does it cross the full width of the lumen, or stop short? Then choose again.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so test the fold's reach across the lumen: haustra do not cross the full width.

say.text: Same film, one more look. Choose again.
Valvulae conniventes do cross the full width, but they mark the small bowel, not the colon.
Large bowel lies peripherally and shows haustra that stop short of the lumen. A large-bowel label needs haustra.
Haustra are real, but they are the colon's marker, and they stop short of the lumen.
The folds on this film cross the full width. That is the small bowel's valvulae conniventes.
Yes. Valvulae conniventes cross the full width and sit in central loops, so this is small bowel.
Haustra never cross the full width. That reach is the feature that separates the two markers.
Two films side by side. Film A: central loops, folds crossing the full width. Film B: peripheral loops, folds that stop short of the lumen.
Film B is the colon. Which feature settles which film is which?

choices.label: Whether any fold is visible at all
Whether the folds cross the full width

say.text: Tempting: every film has some fold, so spotting a fold feels like the marker. Both bowels have folds, so presence does not separate them.
What differs is reach: valvulae cross the full width and mark small bowel; haustra stop short and mark colon.
Yes. Folds that cross the full width are valvulae conniventes, so film A is small bowel.
Film B has folds that stop short, which is the haustral pattern of colon.
By the 3-6-9 rule, what is the upper normal calibre of the caecum on a plain film?
Tempting: 3 is the first number of the rule, so it feels like the caecum's place in a sequence you memorised.
The caecum is the widest of the three segments. Which number goes with the widest one? Then choose again.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so re-anchor the number to calibre: 3 belongs to the narrowest segment, the small bowel.

say.text: Tempting: 6 is the middle value, and a middle number feels like a safe guess for a segment you cannot place.
Count the segments from narrow to wide: small bowel, colon, caecum. Which number matches the widest one? Then choose again.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check which segment 6 belongs to: the colon, the middle of the three.

say.text: Same question. Choose again.
3 cm is the small bowel's upper normal, the narrowest of the three segments.
You gave the narrow end's number to the widest segment. Calibre rises from 3 to 6 to 9 along the gut.
6 cm is the colon's upper normal, not the caecum's.
The caecum is the widest segment and the first to perforate, so it takes the largest number.
Yes. Small bowel 3, colon 6, caecum 9. The numbers rise with calibre.
The caecum is the widest segment, so it has the largest upper limit.
Film report: small bowel 4 cm, transverse colon 5 cm, caecum 7 cm. Which segment is dilated?
Tempting: the caecum at 7 cm looks big next to the other two numbers.
But the caecum's upper normal is 9 cm, so 7 cm is within normal. Only the small bowel, at 4 cm against 3, is above its limit.
Tempting: the transverse colon at 5 cm sits near the middle of the numbers, so it feels large.
The colon's upper normal is 6 cm, so 5 cm is normal. Only the small bowel is dilated here.
Yes. Small bowel at 4 cm is above its 3 cm limit, while colon at 5 cm and caecum at 7 cm are under 6 and 9.
Plain film: a massively dilated loop arising from the pelvis, shaped like a coffee bean. What is the diagnosis?
Tempting: both are a volvulus of a dilated loop, and the caecum is the other big loop people remember.
But this loop arises from the pelvis and looks like a coffee bean. Caecal volvulus gives a comma-shaped caecum displaced to the left upper quadrant.
Yes. A massive pelvic loop with a coffee-bean or bent-inner-tube sign is sigmoid volvulus.
Caecal volvulus shows a kidney-shaped caecum in the left upper quadrant instead.
Each sign belongs to one disease and one modality. Which pairing is correct?

choices.label: Claw sign: ultrasound; pseudokidney: contrast enema
Claw sign: contrast enema; target sign: ultrasound
Bird's beak: intussusception on enema; target: plain film

say.text: Tempting: both signs look like bowel folding back on itself, so the modality is easy to swap in memory.
The claw is the contrast-enema sign of intussusception. The pseudokidney is the ultrasound longitudinal sign. Swapping the modalities puts each sign on the wrong test.
Tempting: bird's beak and claw both appear on an enema, so the enema looks like the common thread.
Bird's beak is the contrast-enema sign of sigmoid volvulus, not of intussusception. Target is an ultrasound sign, not a plain-film sign.
Yes. The claw is the enema sign of intussusception, and the target is the ultrasound sign of the same disease.
Bird's beak belongs to volvulus on contrast enema, so keep each sign on its own disease and test.
An adult with suspected small bowel obstruction. Which is the definitive investigation, the test that gives the level and the cause?
Tempting: the plain film is the first test you order, and it does show the dilated bowel, so it feels complete.
It shows that the bowel is blocked. Which test shows where the block is and what is causing it? Then choose again.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate the two jobs: the film says obstruction is present, and a different test answers level and cause.

say.text: Tempting: a barium meal is a classic contrast study of the gut, so it feels like the definitive test.
Think about what barium would do if the bowel were perforated or the colon were blocked. Then choose again.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so note the danger: barium is unsafe when there is perforation or large bowel obstruction.

say.text: Same question, one more try. Choose again.
The plain film is the initial investigation: it confirms obstruction and shows which bowel is dilated.
It does not give the level, the cause or the signs of strangulation. Contrast CT does, so it is the definitive test.
Barium must not be given in suspected large bowel obstruction or perforation, so it is not the test to reach for here.
In adhesive obstruction a water-soluble oral contrast study can be diagnostic and therapeutic, but that is not barium.
Yes. Contrast CT is the investigation of choice for small bowel obstruction: it shows the level, the cause and signs of strangulation.
The plain film is the initial test, and CT is the definitive one.
Three rungs, in order: initial test for suspected obstruction; definitive test for small bowel obstruction; diagnostic test for a child with suspected intussusception.
Which ladder is right?
Tempting: CT is the definitive test, so putting it first feels efficient, and the enema is a familiar test for a child.
The ladder runs from the test that confirms obstruction to the one that gives level and cause. Ultrasound, not enema, is the child's diagnostic test.
Yes. Plain film first, then contrast CT for the definitive answer, then ultrasound for a child with suspected intussusception.
Each test answers a different question, so the order is the ladder.
